issues.title: RFC1035 doesn't say MUST NOT
issues.author: nidhijaju
issues.body:
https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-gakiwate-dnsop-optimistic-dns-00.html#section-8.1-1 claims:
> The DNS specifications require that DNS records with a TTL of zero MUST NOT be cached [[RFC1035](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-gakiwate-dnsop-optimistic-dns-00.html#RFC1035)].

Since RFC1035 predates RFC2119, perhaps we can just quote the text itself:
```
TTL             a 32 bit signed integer that specifies the time interval
                that the resource record may be cached before the source
                of the information should again be consulted.  Zero
                values are interpreted to mean that the RR can only be
                used for the transaction in progress, and should not be
                cached.  For example, SOA records are always distributed
                with a zero TTL to prohibit caching.  Zero values can
                also be used for extremely volatile data.
```

issues.title: Section 8 (Interaction with Other DNS Features) doesn't mention SVCB records (especially ECH)
issues.author: nidhijaju
issues.body:
[RFC9460 Section 9.2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9460.html#name-cache-lifetime) states: 

> Some DNS caches incorrectly extend the lifetime of DNS records beyond the stated TTL, so server operators cannot rely on HTTPS RRs expiring on time. Shortening the TTL to compensate for incorrect caching is NOT RECOMMENDED, as this practice impairs the performance of correctly functioning caches and does not guarantee faster expiration from incorrect caches. Instead, server operators SHOULD maintain compatibility with expired records until they observe that nearly all connections have migrated to the new configuration.

Optimistic DNS is essentially doing what RFC9460 claims is "incorrect". I think most of the SvcParams are fine, but for SVCB/HTTPS records with an `ech=` SvcParam, a stale ECHConfig means the server cannot decrypt the ClientHelloInner, so the server falls back via `retry_configs`, and the client must retry, costing a roundtrip. Not sure if this matters, but an on-path attacker can also observe these retries and potentially infer past behavior about the client.

Additionally, since clients with an ECHConfig [should fail closed](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9849.html#section-8.1.1-3) and not send unencrypted ClientHellos, we probably should add some guidance around replacing an Optimistic Answer with an ECHConfig with a fresh answer even if it doesn't contain an ECHConfig, since otherwise clients may be blocked for the entire duration the stub resolver is willing to return stale answers.

Perhaps we should add text to Section 8 outlining that to stay compatible with RFC9460 and RFC9849, we should not use Optimstic DNS for SVCB/HTTPS records with a non-empty `ech=` SvcParamKey.

issues.title: Missing privacy considerations
issues.author: nidhijaju
issues.body:
We should have a privacy considerations section (potentially following RFC6973). A few topics that seem good to cover: 

* Cache timing attacks by co-located applications
* Persistence of cached data past its original TTL
* Stale-while-refreshing behavior observable to on-path observers and recursive resolvers
* SNI leakage to incorrect destinations after using a stale answer that turns out to be wrong
* Risks of caching cross-network (reinforce that we still shouldn't)

issues.title: Update terminology to be more consistent
issues.author: nidhijaju
issues.body:
Throughout the document, we use "Optimistic DNS Client" without defining it. Perhaps "Optimistic DNS Client" could be defined as "An application or networking library that has signaled to the stub resolver that it is prepared to receive Optimistic Answers."

We also use "fresh", "current", and "fresh new" to refer to non-staleness.
We can also clarify "Optimistic Positive Answer" and "Optimistic Negative Answer" to make it clear that this is a Positive or Negative Answer that happens to be Optimistic, rather than Positive/Negative applying to the Optimistic part.

There's already a good terminology section that defines the other terms, so this is likely a minor update and we can do an editorial pass for consistency.

issues.title: Section 7.4: Cache managements with multiple networks/PvDs
issues.author: stefanoduo-google
issues.body:
As briefly highlighted in Section 3, a device awaking from sleep is a common scenario where Optimistic DNS makes a real difference in user perceived latency. In this scenario it's not always obvious whether the device is still using the same PvD it was previously using. While cross-PvD DNS cache management is technically orthogonal to this draft, Optimistic DNS might exacerbate "cross-network contamination" (this has also been mentioned also in issue #4); which, for the reasons stated in RFCs 6418, 6731, 7556; is not recommended.

Section 7.4 gives the following recommendation for cache management:
> stub resolvers SHOULD NOT store records for more than X after the TTL has expired

Should it also say something about cross-PvD cache management? Perhaps we could just refer to RFC 8801, which attempts to solve this with PvD IDs for explicit PvDs.

issues.title: Extend dependency re-evaluation to SVCB/HTTPS resolution
issues.author: bashi
issues.body:
Section 7.5 specifies rewind-and-restart behavior for CNAME chains. SVCB/HTTPS resolution creates a similar dependency graph: AliasMode chains, ServiceMode RRs and SvcParams, TargetName A/AAAA records, and address hints.

An update to any dependency can change the valid endpoint configuration even when the final address set is unchanged. Implementations should re-evaluate the original service query and notify the client whenever the resulting service-binding configuration changes.

This issue concerns general resolution consistency. The policy for using stale ech SvcParams and ECH-specific security/privacy considerations is tracked separately in #3.

issues.title: Consider a confirmation callback when a fresh answer matches the expired answer
issues.author: bashi
issues.body:
Section 6 currently says:

> When a fresh positive answer matches the previous Optimistic Positive Answer,
> no second callback is delivered.

I think "no callback" might be ambiguous for the application. After receiving "Optimistic Positive Answer", it cannot tell whether the fresh answer arrived and matched, the network query is still in flight, or the query failed.

This matters most in the window where the application is still listening. For example, the connection attempt to the stale address (203.0.113.34 in the example) is hanging or being reset, and the fresh answer returns the same address. Under the current text the application receives nothing, so it keeps waiting in case a corrected address is about to arrive. With a confirmation it would know the address is correct and the host is just down, and it could fail fast.

The confirmation could also help while the TCP/TLS handshake is still in progress. Once the application knows the address was confirmed, it can stop treating the ongoing attempt as provisional, for example by restoring the normal timeout or releasing resources reserved for retrying with a corrected address. Note that when the fresh answer changes but still contains the address in use, the application does get a callback, so it can confirm the address. Only the fully unchanged case, which confirms the address most strongly, gives the application no signal.

The draft already accepts this reasoning for the negative case.

> Sending confirmations of Optimistic Negative Answers is necessary because
> the client may be waiting for that negative answer confirmation before
> proceeding with its next steps.

The same logic seems to apply to positive answers, so I wonder if this asymmetry is intentional.

comments.author: gakiwate
gakiwate
comments.body:
Thanks again @nidhijaju. I went ahead and pushed the style tweak to your branch so this can land.

One wrinkle with the wording I suggested earlier: `{{Section 3.2.1 of !RFC1035}}` expands to "Section 3.2.1 of [RFC1035]", so "The DNS specification {{Section 3.2.1 of !RFC1035}} states that ..." would have rendered as "The DNS specification Section 3.2.1 of [RFC1035] states that ...". Moving the citation into a trailing parenthetical keeps the reference out of the noun slot and still reads cleanly:

> The DNS specification states that DNS records with a TTL of zero "can only be used for the transaction in progress, and should not be cached" (Section 3.2.1 of [RFC1035]). This document does not change that guidance; subsequent queries for these records always result in a new network request.

Merging now. Thanks for catching the incorrect `MUST NOT` attribution.

pulls.title: Add Firefox to the Optimistic DNS deployment history
pulls.author: mxinden
pulls.body:
@gakiwate as discussed, adding a Firefox section. Depends on https://github.com/mozilla/happy-eyeballs/issues/125 and Happy Eyeballs v3 landing in Firefox Release ([tracking issue](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1953459)). I expect this to happen soon, i.e. before this draft publishes.

---

Document Firefox's client-side optimistic DNS in two layers, alongside the mDNSResponder section.

The stub resolver (nsHostResolver) has served expired records within a grace period, revalidating them in the background, by default since Firefox 18 (January 2013). Describe its three record states, negative revalidation, and the grace window, which began at thirty days and now defaults to ten minutes.

The Happy Eyeballs v3 state machine emits a query that allows a stale answer, races connections on the expired record it gets back, and emits a second query that bars the cache to force a fresh lookup, updating its candidate addresses when the fresh answer arrives. This applies the draft's asynchronous model and per-query signaling.

Add an informative reference to the Firefox stub resolver source.

pulls.title: Add initial draft of Android's APIs and cover the security implication of SNI leaks
pulls.author: fridek
pulls.body:
Adds Android's section modelled after https://github.com/gakiwate/draft-gakiwate-dnsop-optimistic-dns/pull/9

It does cover options that are in use but are not a part of Optimistic DNS proposal so feel free to suggest trimming it down to fit the format better. 
We let apps wait for the first request to complete and set a timeout (`setFreshLookupTimeout`) when the stale value would be used. Effectively, this draft proposes that `0` is a reasonable default, which I agree with.
`setAllowCrossNetworkUsage` and `setUseStaleOnNameNotResolved` are, in my opinion not in scope of Optimistic DNS (instead draft-kinnear-dnsop-globally-relevant). It works well for services that use anycast but is not a reasonable default behaviour. 
I left the text in as a note, but we might want to omit it completely.

Also added a section on potential SNI leaks and suggestion to use of ECH to mitigate

comments.author: gakiwate
comments.body:
Thanks @fridek. This is excellent. I took you up on the offer to trim this to the document's shape. I have made some suggested edits for you to consider. Please look at them and see if you have any follow up comments or further edits.

- I took the liberty to add a reference to `DnsOptions.StaleDnsOptions`. I also used the Android Developer documentation for  `StaleDnsOptions` to flesh out the `setFreshLookupTimeout` and `setMaxExpiredDelay`.
- I agree with your read on setAllowCrossNetworkUsage and setUseStaleOnNameNotResolved. Talking about results from another network's DNS server is  broader than the expired record mechanism here.
- I also heavily edited the SNI/ECH text (if you can review that would be appreciated). The exposure you identified is real and is still addressed in the draft elsewhere. Section 7.1 already says applications without Happy Eyeballs and application-layer security SHOULD NOT use Optimistic DNS, so a stronger requirement is redundant. Moreover, SNI and ECH exist only in TLS, so the leak and a TLS-only fix were both attached to the unencrypted case.

comments.author: gakiwate
comments.body: @fridek I am merging in the text. If you feel the text misrepresents anything please let me know and we can fix it.
